newsitem.title: USA: North American power grid braces for solar storm.
newsitem.headline: North American power grid braces for solar storm.

text.p: Power companies in the northern U.S. and Canada said Wednesday they are bracing for a solar storm later today that, if severe, could knock out their generating and transmission systems.

"It has the potential to produce a severe impact on the power system...and the potential to produce large area blackouts," said John Kappenman, supervisor of transmission power engineering at Minnesota Power in Duluth.
"But this is an immature science. Forecasting these phenomena is extremely frustrating, with only about a 30 percent accuracy range," he said.
"With 93 million miles of inner-planetary space to cross, that's a lot of uncertainty."

The call to action came from the National Aeronatics and Space Administration (NASA), which earlier Wednesday said a large storm on the sun's surface probably would hit the earth's magnetic field later today.

The solar storm was detected about 48 hours ago by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, a WIND companion satellite that NASA and the European Space Agency launched in 1995 to keep a constant eye on the sun's surface.
A similar storm caused widespread disturbances on the North American power system on March 13, 1989.
It hit the utility Hydro Quebec especially hard, plunging Quebec's five million residents into the dark and nearly toppling the power grid in parts of the U.S. Northeast.
Kappenman said nations close to the magnetic north pole are most exposed to such phenomena, called geomagnetic disturbances.

The disturbances occur when ionized solar particles collide with the earth's magnetic field, disturbing typically stable magnetic fields on the earth's surface and increasing the flow of direct current electricity through the ground.

Taking the path of least resistance, these currents flow to grounding cables at power facilities, entering substation transformers and moving onto high-voltage lines, making it difficult in extreme cases to regulate the grid's voltage.

The problem is most pronounced in regions with large deposits of igneous rock, a hard rock that does not conduct electricty well, making it more likely the direct current will find its way to a grounding cable.

According to the North American Electricity Reliability Council (NERC), the areas most likely to see geomagnetic distrubrances are the Pacific Northwest, the Rockies, the upper Midwest, eastern Canada and the East Coast as far south as Washington DC.
What steps can be taken to protect the power grid from geomagnetic disturbances?
"Generally, we are trying to harden the system for anticipated impact on voltage regulation," said Kappenman.
"Which means we might reduce power being carried over long distances, instead powering up local power generation to provide more local voltage stability."

He said Minnesota Power was feeling especially vulnerable to any voltage fluctuations since many of the region's transmission lines are currently down, knocked out by the blizzard that struck the region earlier this week.

Gene Gorzelnik, director of communications at Princeton, N.J.-based NERC headquarters, said most power companies would likely pay extra close attention to ground currents at their units and perhaps trim loads on their systems, if necessary.
"But remember, solar flares are a normal occurance...This is a potential event, something that could happen. But it's not the Second Coming," Gorzelnik said.
((--New York Power Desk - 212 859 1621))
